questions.q: If $49^n+16^n+k$ is divisible by 64 for $n \in N$, then the least negative integral value of $k$ is
questions.solution:
Let $P(n)=49^n+16^n+k$
For $n=1$, we get
$P(1)=49^{(1)}+16^{(1)}+k=65+k$
As $P(1)$ is divisible by 64 , we take
$k=-1P(1)=65-1=64$, which is divisible by 64 .
Thus, the least negative integral value of $k$ be -1 .

Let $P(k)=2^{3 k}-7 k-1=49 t$, where $t$ is an integer
Now,
$\begin{aligned}
P(k+1) & =2^{3(k+1)}-7(k+1)-1=2^{3 k} \cdot 2^3-7 k-7-1 \\

Thus, $2^{3 n}-7 n-1$ is divisible by 49 .

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Using mathematical induction, the numbers $a_n \delta$ are defined by $a_0=1, a_{n+1}=3 n^2+n+a_n, (n \geq 0)$. Then, $a_n$ is equal to
questions.solution:
The recurrence relation is given by $a_{n+1} = a_n + 3n^2 + n$ with $a_0 = 1$.

We can write the general term $a_n$ as a summation:

$a_n = a_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (a_{k+1} - a_k) = 1 + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (3k^2 + k)$.

Using the standard summation formulas $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k^2 = \dfrac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6}$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k = \dfrac{(n-1)n}{2}$, we substitute these into the expression for $a_n$:

$a_n = 1 + 3 \left[ \dfrac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6} \right] + \dfrac{(n-1)n}{2}$.

Simplifying the expression:

$a_n = 1 + \dfrac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{2} + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = 1 + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} [ (2n-1) + 1 ]$.

$a_n = 1 + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} [ 2n ] = 1 + n^2(n-1) = 1 + n^3 - n^2$.

Thus, $a_n = n^3 - n^2 + 1$.

Answer: $n^3-n^2+1$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $f(n) = 2^{3n} - 7n - 1 = 8^n - 7n - 1$.

Using the binomial expansion, $8^n = (1 + 7)^n = 1 + ^{n}C_{1}(7) + ^{n}C_{2}(7^2) + ^{n}C_{3}(7^3) + \dots + ^{n}C_{n}(7^n)$.

Substituting this into the expression for $f(n)$:

$f(n) = (1 + 7n + ^{n}C_{2}(49) + ^{n}C_{3}(7^3) + \dots + 7^n) - 7n - 1$.

$f(n) = ^{n}C_{2}(49) + ^{n}C_{3}(7^3) + \dots + 7^n$.

Since every term in the expansion contains at least $49$ as a factor, $f(n)$ is divisible by $49$.

Answer: 49

questions.q: Using mathematical induction, the numbers $a_{n}$ 's are defined by $a_{0}=1, a_{n+1}=3 n^{2}+n+a_{n}$, $(n \geq 0)$. Then, $a_{n}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given the recurrence relation $a_{n+1} = a_{n} + 3n^{2} + n$ with $a_{0} = 1$.

We can write the terms as:
$a_{n} = a_{0} + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (a_{k+1} - a_{k})$

$a_{n} = 1 + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (3k^{2} + k)$

Using the standard summation formulas $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k^{2} = \dfrac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6}$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k = \dfrac{(n-1)n}{2}$:

$a_{n} = 1 + 3 \left[ \dfrac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6} \right] + \dfrac{(n-1)n}{2}$

$a_{n} = 1 + \dfrac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{2} + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$

$a_{n} = 1 + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} [ (2n-1) + 1 ]$

$a_{n} = 1 + \dfrac{n(n-1)(2n)}{2}$

$a_{n} = 1 + n^{2}(n-1)$

$a_{n} = 1 + n^{3} - n^{2}$

Answer: $n^{3}-n^{2}+1$

questions.q: The remainder obtained when $(1 !)^{2}+(2 !)^{2}+(3 !)^{2}+\ldots+(100 !)^{2}$ is divided by $10^{2}$ is
questions.solution:
Here, terms greater than $5 !$, i.e. $(5 !)^{2},(6 !)^{2}, \ldots \ldots,(100 !)^{2}$ is divisible by 100 .
$\therefore$ For terms
$(5 !)^{2},(6 !)^{2}, \ldots(100 !)^{2}$ remainder is 0 .
Now, consider $(1 !)^{2}+(2 !)^{2}+(3 !)^{2}+(4 !)^{2}=1+4+36+576=617$
When, 617 is divided by 100 , its remainder is 17 . So, required remainder is 17 .

questions.q: In the group $G=\{1,5,7,11\}$ under multiplication modulo 12, the solution of $7^{-1} \underset{12}{\times}(x \underset{12}{12} 11)=5$ is $x=$
questions.solution:
Given that, $G=\{1,5,7,11\}$ is a group under multiplication module 12 .
$\because \quad 7^{-1}=7 \quad\left[\because 7^{-1} \otimes_{12} 7=1\right]\begin{array}{ll}\text { Now, } & 7^{-1} \otimes_{12}\left(x \otimes_{12} 11\right)=5 \\ \Rightarrow & 7 \otimes_{12}\left(11 \otimes_{12} x\right)=5 \\ \Rightarrow & \left(7 \otimes_{12} 11\right) \otimes_{12} x=5 \\ \Rightarrow & \left\{7 \otimes_{12} 11=\text { remainder after dividing } 77 \text { from } 12\right\} \\ \Rightarrow & 5 \otimes_{12} x=5 \\ \Rightarrow & x=1\end{array}$

We have, $583 ! \equiv 0(\bmod 10)$
and $\quad 7^{2}=-1(\bmod 10)$
So, $\left(7^{2}\right)^{145} \cdot 7^{1}=(-1)^{145} \cdot 7^{1}(\bmod 10)\Rightarrow \quad 7^{291}=-7(\bmod 10) \equiv 3(\bmod 10)$
So, $583 !+7^{291}=3(\bmod 10)$
Hence, last digit is $3 .$
